figures.caption: Figure 3: OpenPLC/MATIEC as behavioral reference. OpenPLC uses MATIEC [11] to compile IEC 61131-3 to C and runs it on a scan loop. MATIEC supplies reference C implementations of standard function blocks (TON, TOF, TP, CTU, CTD) driven by elapsed time. As these run on deployed open-hardware PLCs, their per-scan behavior is the reference for validating K-ESBMC’s blocks, and the tie-breaker when a verifier and K-ESBMC disagree.

Figure 4: Positioning on the assurance/effort spectrum. Rather than full verified compilation [18] or translation validation [19], we adopt differential testing [22] against an executable reference, supported by machine-checked per-construct lemmas. K’s dual generation of interpreter and prover from a single semantics – as with C [13] and the EVM [17] – enables both testing and proving. Our contribution is adapting this approach to a verifier’s front-end in a safety-critical domain.

Table 2: K-ESBMC versus representative IEC 61131-3 semantics and verification tools. “Executable” = runs programs to produce concrete traces; “Oracle” = usable to validate another tool’s translation; “Runtime-validated” = checked against a deployed PLC runtime.

Figure 5: The three-engine differential. Each PLCopen benchmark is verified by ESBMC (the translation under test) and, independently, executed by the K-ESBMC oracle via frontends that never reuse ESBMC’s parser; verdicts are compared. On any disagreement, the OpenPLC/MATIEC runtime – against which K-ESBMC is validated scan-for-scan (RQ1) – is the external tie-breaker.

Figure 1: K-ESBMC in one picture. A graphical LD rung is given an operational meaning as a set of K rewrite rules – extending K-ST, the K semantics of ST, with contacts, coils, the scan cycle, timers, counters, and edge blocks. From that single definition, K yields, for free, both an interpreter (krun) that runs diagrams scan by scan and a program verifier (kprove). Because K-ESBMC executes, its fidelity is checked directly, scan for scan, against a reference PLC runtime.

Table 5: Three-engine differential over the benchmark suite. K-ESBMC verdicts list the violated properties. Rows marked × disagree; all three are resolved in K-ESBMC’s favor in §5.3.

Figure 2: Where K-ESBMC fits in K. K defines a language as a configuration (cells) plus rewrite rules, deriving both an interpreter (krun) and a prover (kprove) from one definition. K covers C, Java, JavaScript, and the EVM. For IEC 61131-3, Wang et al. [21] give K-ST for ST; K-ESBMC shares the framework and scan cycle but adds LD and its function blocks, which K-ST omits.
